title: Systems and emergence
thesis: Roguelikes get their depth from systems that interact under one consistent set of rules, so that the player keeps meeting problems nobody scripted and solving them with ingenuity. The designer's real decisions are what to simulate and what it says, how many pieces to have and how densely they connect, and how to build the architecture that lets them combine. The same openness produces exploits, runaway loops and invisible stories, so a good systemic designer also chooses which leaks to keep, which to plug and how to make the simulation legible.

sections.heading: Why roguelikes are built from interacting systems
sections.brief: Open with the case for systems as the genre's engine: Brian Walker's chain of exciting situations and Darren Grey's escalating threat met by clever use of items converge on the idea that the player must keep solving new problems, and Dan Recht adds that interacting systems force trade-offs no player can master all at once. Then show where the new problems come from: George Moromisato's contrast between NetHack's combinatorial breadth and chess's depth, Alice Lai's argument that combos count as content alongside monsters and biomes, and Mike Cook's point that designers only set rules while the action space outgrows them. Gather the emergence-from-simple-rules material (Lazer-Walker's Life gliders, Joel Clark on Blaseball surprising its own developers, Devereux's biology, Nat Alison's L-systems and Go, Lee Tusman) as one convergent strand, and set Biskup's 'interaction' as core mechanic beside Josh Ge's report that NetHack's core mechanic is 'if it seems possible, it is'. End with guidance: treat interactions as content, design for the player's ingenuity, and keep the clever options visible rather than buried in junk (Grey).

sections.heading: One rule set for player, monster and world
sections.brief: Argue that emergence depends on consistency: the Adams brothers' creature files that define a dwarf like an emu, Derek Yu's shared rule set as what makes Spelunky a roguelike (via Tyriq Plummer), droqen's teleporter that treats blocks, monsters and the player alike, Dustin Freeman's 'peership' and Rich Wilson's rule that every placed object carry its full systemic properties all say the same thing, and the section should show that convergence. Include the consequences of taking it seriously: Cataclysm's 'if it works in reality it works in the game', Caves of Qud giving even a door a body and inventory, NetHack killing a player who genocides their own class, HyperRogue's shops as ordinary map space. Then widen from rules to a world that does not revolve around the player: Cogmind's busy robots, Qud's factions warring without you, Bad News routines, Lessard's god game that carries on if you do nothing, against Max Kreminski's warnings about solipsism and extractive play and his questions about worlds that run while you're away. End with practical guidance on removing special cases for the player and giving the world its own business.

sections.heading: Choosing what to simulate: theme, emphasis and values
sections.brief: Argue that picking systems is picking what the game says. Start with Brenda Romero listing a setting's systems before designing traits and her point that which system you emphasise changes the whole game; then Jongwoo Kim's discovery that materialist simulation references undermined The Shrouded Isle's spiritual theme, so food and shelter became virtues and house opinion. Stage the warnings that systems speak whether you mean them to: Grinblat's 'combat gravity well' (relayed by Ivy Melinda), Lazer-Walker on kill-as-main-verb, Walker cutting Brogue's vomit-drains-food gag, Xalavier Nelson refusing size-based organ values, Brough on Vancian magic drifting to mana points, and Darren Grey on copying the hunger clock without a reason. Then the constructive routes: Ludipe's cheap reskin versus harder theme-derived systems, Devereux and Niche turning biology into mechanics, Pipkin on digging as a mechanic whose purpose varies, Rabii's Tea Garden where one interaction turned flowers into hats, and Jeff Lait's claim that a roguelike's art lives in its systems. End with questions a designer should ask of each system: what it rewards, what it says, and why it is there.

sections.heading: How many pieces: dense interactions versus sprawling content
sections.brief: Set up the central disagreement: Eric Billingsley and Michael Brough argue for few elements tuned to interact densely (Brough's four enemy types in 868-HACK, type-specific effects only mattering when types are few), while the NetHack tradition from the first section and Casey Yano's move to unlimited relics in Slay the Spire show the case for breadth and accumulation. Bring in Brough's craft points as concrete technique: one exception to a rule is magic but two imply a new rule, effects that twist a situation (polymorph) beat strictly better or worse ones, and 868-HACK's warp shows how to tame variance. Tom Francis's shuffle-friendly design (rich cards rather than a clever shuffle; tools, enemy traits and global filters) and Tim Keenan's per-run content subsets show how to get variety from recombination. Evan Debenham's layered simple systems and active over passive effects, Dan Norder on Chase's minimalism, Shiren's day/night modes that split the player base, and Johnathon Pagnutti on matching complexity to the audience round it out. End with guidance on choosing a density and on cutting elements that don't interact.

sections.heading: Uncertainty: randomness, hidden information and the simulated dice
sections.brief: Argue that randomness in a systemic game works best when it stands for something. Aaron Reed's constrained randomness (Oregon Trail's mileage-weighted events encoding geography) and Nic Tringali's account of dice as everything the game doesn't simulate frame the section; set against them Xalavier Nelson's finding that a market forced to make sense felt less real than true randomness. Then map the sources of uncertainty: Shawn Main's list and Andrea Roberts' call for new ones (gambling, climate models, divination), Chogue's darkness turning chess into survival horror, Tringali on how dice and decks depend on what players know, Cezar Capacle's 'structured randomness' procedures, and Nick Cummings on how sheer volume of repeated play breeds strange outcomes. Rogue's deliberate quirks to break Rog-O-Matic and NetHack's fake mail are small colour. End with guidance on choosing where uncertainty enters and tying random draws to the simulation's state.

sections.heading: Architectures that let everything interact
sections.brief: This is the implementation section and should be specific enough to build from. Lead with the convergent answer to combinatorial explosion: don't code pairs of objects, code properties. George Moromisato on NetHack's shared materials and resistances and on forces acting on materials in a data-driven engine, Rich Wilson's stimulus-and-response model from immersive sims, Thomas Biskup's Lego-like externalised components and body parts that grant capabilities, and Liza Knipscher's Bioloom deriving behaviour from body parts are the same idea at different scales. Then the variants: Scott Kovach's rule-based system where independent authors' rules compose into boots burning over lava, Kate Compton on The Sims' advertised needs as pure data, Tarn Adams on a generalised villain network that repairs itself locally and that the player can reuse, Biskup's relative item sizes, and Reed's Hobbit checking goal states rather than solutions. End with a short list of patterns and what each costs.

sections.heading: Terrain, materials and physical simulation
sections.brief: Start with Brian Walker's claim that rich terrain beats monsters because it is self-explanatory and supports plans, then Brogue's techniques (one spreading-terrain mechanic, gas averaged over neighbours, and gravity for liquids, gases and collapse), Darren Grey on feeling roguish by using external power, and the Cataclysm and Caves of Qud chains where fire, steam and noise create tactics. Give the implementation detail of cellular-automaton material systems from Scott Anderson (six base movement rules, neighbour 'alchemy', probability tuning, bottom-up update order, density swaps) alongside Ian Holmes's history and stochastic prototypes and Noita's pixel physics. Then stage the problems: Arvi Teikari on destruction becoming boring and on simulated reactions that don't become decisions, set against Rich Wilson's prediction that ever finer simulation shifts the burden to designers. Close with guidance on choosing which physical properties to simulate and how to make them readable and decision-relevant.

sections.heading: Items, magic and hazards built to combine
sections.brief: Argue that items, spells and hazards earn their place by what they do in combination. John Harris's 'creative application of every trick' in Mystery Dungeon games and Reed Lockwood's rule that traps must tie into other systems frame it; Nick McConnell's Angband traps that degenerated into a detection check show what happens otherwise. Then the techniques and cases: Biskup's Ultimate ADOM magic (animating walls and altars, grafting limbs, crystal chain reactions), Joris Dormans and Sersa Victory's networked plant hazards with lingering consequences and remote solutions in Bane, Caves of Qud's evil twin and psychic hunters as threats that scale with the player's own power, Spencer Egart's ritual magic, Wildermyth's scenery-bound mystics, Shiren's mixers, Rift Wizard's friendly fire and snowballing summons, and NetHack's cockatrice, bag of holding, holy water and conflict. End with guidance on giving each new element hooks into existing systems.

sections.heading: Resource systems: what every action costs
sections.brief: Build on Dylan White's framework: renewability and fungibility as the two questions about any resource, with his examples (mana versus per-spell charges, cooldowns as tiny mana bars, DCSS layering mana with piety) and his refusal to name a correct answer. Then show resources that do double duty: Desktop Dungeons regenerating only when you explore, Caves of Qud's water as thirst clock and currency, Reigns' resources that kill at both extremes (via Jongwoo Kim), Roguelight's arrows as light and weapon, Darkest Dungeon's stress, and Harris's use-now-or-later items. The Banished Vault's physical, distance-scaled logistics and Jeff Lait's 'hidden growth' pattern (Smith's Hand) show resources as a source of pressure over time. End with practical guidance: name your resource system, say what behaviour it encourages, and check that its costs produce decisions.

sections.heading: Prices, trade and simulated economies
sections.brief: Ask whether an economy should be simulated at all: Mark Gritter's question of whether trade changes the world or is decoration, and his techniques (goods with several uses, diminishing utility, auction-based trade finding) together with his view that visible suboptimal outcomes are fine if players can act on them. Set Robin Mendoza's warning that prices pull players out of spatial situations into abacus calculation, and his question of whether markets are redundant beside magic, against his own praise for two currencies in 868-HACK and fixed exchange rates as valuation heuristics. Xalavier Nelson's organ market (easily systematised goods) and resource-trade choices in ADOM and NetHack (via Sersa Victory) are the cases. End with guidance on when a price system adds decisions and when it only adds arithmetic.

sections.heading: Characters, relationships and social simulation
sections.brief: Argue that the richest systems are often about people. Jongwoo Kim's move in The Shrouded Isle from aggregate house orders to specific characters, and his reading of Crusader Kings II, lead; Cat Manning's orthogonal traits in Dwarf Fortress, Jim Shepard's like/respect relationship values, Dustin Freeman's grudges outliving their cause and Max Kreminski's Star Freighter crew moods all show how small values produce scripted-feeling moments. Caves of Qud's water ritual, faction reputation tied to generated backstories and its etiquette rule show a social system as gameplay; Mark Johnson's dialect disguise, Fire Emblem: Three Houses' story-combat loop and Leigh Alexander on reality TV as a drama generator widen the frame. End with guidance on decoupling traits and on letting relationships change the player's options.

sections.heading: Emergent stories and making the simulation legible
sections.brief: Start with Rich Wilson's 'church of the simulation': events produced by impartial systems feel like they happened. Show the convergent canon of emergent anecdotes (Brogue's incineration-potion bridge, the Demonspawn whose hooves shed his flying boots, Dwarf Fortress's drunk cats) and then stage Emilia Lazer-Walker's objection that the drunk cats are a story of the simulation, not the player. The legibility problem follows: Cat Manning's sliding scale for surfacing causes, Jonathan Lessard on deep simulations whose history players never see, Caves of Qud's layered generators producing coherent-seeming villages, and Sunshine Shuffle players projecting motives onto an AI. Brenda Romero on Wizardry players inventing relationships, the Adams brothers' persistent killers and Jamie Brittain on NetHack's cat add colour. End with guidance on deciding how much the game should explain and on surfacing causes.

sections.heading: Leak or fountain: bugs, exploits and players who break the system
sections.brief: Centre the section on Jason Grinblat's argument: in emergent games rough edges signal a possibility space too big to file down ('the dev team does not think of everything'), so ask before fixing whether a leak is a fountain, as with Qud's body-swap exploit kept as a feature. Set this against DCSS's codified philosophy of removing powerful but tedious options (Alan Malloy on victory dancing) and against NetHack's long history with polypiling and pudding farming (Kawa, the DevTeam's choice to add risk rather than ban it), so the reader sees what each choice depends on. Bring in Blaseball as the extreme fountain position (keeping broken systems, the dead player brought back wrong, community as co-author), Brenda Romero's relationship bugs, Courtney Liessen on soft boundaries, Cat Manning on leaning into simulation weaknesses, and Florence Smith Nicholls on glitches as prompts for sharing. Edge cases (Qud's overburdened start, Crawl's Royal Jelly vault, NetHack's fake amulet in bones), player exploits (Against the Storm fences, leprechaun gold), and self-imposed constraints (conducts, Kruggsmash's ocean fort, the Adams brothers' Elbereth ban) are support. End with a triage rule of thumb for bugs and exploits.

sections.heading: Keeping emergent systems tunable and under control
sections.brief: The counterweight to the previous section: systems that run away. Liza Knipscher's Bioloom, where a free reproduction shortcut let fruit-covered flying triceratopses take over, and her rule that the energy economy must have no clever workarounds, lead; Ian Holmes's stochastic-process tools and birth-death models, Jasmine Otto's forward simulation that never stops, Jurie Horneman's warning about untunable cascades of selection, reward and progression, and Arvi Teikari's erratic Noita world are the same problem from different angles. Then robustness: Tarn Adams on letting the player break an investigative thread, Mark Johnson on clues being destroyed, Jim Shepard on pruning events, NetHack scoping eating to one turn, Qud removing fun bugs that burned mountains and cutting powered furniture that implied a system it couldn't deliver. End with practical guidance on caps, costs, pruning and scoping a system to what you can fully deliver.

sections.heading: Systems beyond the single-player dungeon
sections.brief: Collect the frontiers: what happens to systems with more players, at the table, or in live play. Leif Bloomquist's shared-world roguelike (players as the other characters, keys that teleport home, emergent cooperation at a 50-person demo, puzzles needing simultaneous actions) and Tyriq Plummer's Clean Sweep queued co-op actions, set against Plummer's later warning that cascading effects stall multiplayer play. Tabletop and live-action systems: Cole Wehrle's Oath cards that paint rules onto sites and carry them into the next game, Robin Laws' adjective-card resolution system and its digital extensions in Thousand Hells (David Dunham), Yong Zhen Zhou's physical costs, and Dennis Greger's larp techniques for shifting social roles and escalating loops. End with what transfers back to single-player design.
